questions.question: Why is video generation much harder than image generation even if both use diffusion?
options: Because videos cannot be compressed
Because videos add a time dimension, massively increasing data size and the need for temporal consistency
Because diffusion only works on still images
Because prompts are shorter for video
questions.explanation: The lesson starts by pointing out that a video is effectively a 3-D tensor rather than a 2-D image. That adds far more data to process and creates a new requirement: frames must stay coherent over time instead of each being correct in isolation.

questions.question: What artifact do you expect if you generate each frame independently with an image model?
options: Perfect motion tracking
Flicker from frame-to-frame inconsistency
Higher audio quality
Lower memory use with no downside
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that independent per-frame sampling produces flicker. Without coupling frames through shared denoising or attention, identities, lighting, and details drift from one frame to the next.

questions.question: What role does the video VAE play in the lesson's architecture?
options: It writes the final captions for the clip
It compresses the video into spatiotemporal latents before patchification and diffusion
It replaces temporal attention with convolutions
It guarantees full 3D attention is cheap
questions.explanation: The concept section begins with spatiotemporal compression using a 3D VAE. Instead of diffusing raw frames, the model first turns the clip into a smaller latent tensor over time and space, which makes the downstream DiT tractable.

questions.question: Why do production video models usually use factorized attention instead of full 3D attention?
options: Because factorized attention removes the need for positional embeddings
Because full 3D attention is far more expensive, so models separate spatial and temporal attention to control compute
Because text conditioning only works with factorized attention
Because factorized attention requires no training data
questions.explanation: The lesson states that full 3D attention can be 16 to 100 times more expensive and is mostly limited to low-resolution research settings. Splitting attention into spatial and temporal passes keeps the model expressive while staying within practical memory and latency budgets.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what training data improvement was especially important for Sora-style video models?
options: Switching from text prompts to class labels only
Using much more detailed re-captioned clips with dense prompts
Removing all first-frame conditioning examples
Training only on five-second videos
questions.explanation: The pitfalls section says caption quality mattered enormously and highlights GPT-generated dense re-captions. More detailed descriptions gave the model better supervision about actions, objects, and scene changes than short web captions alone.
